title: Alicia in Wonderland: The Red & White Queens
description:
Version 3 (31 October 2026) adds 43 full-page plates after Chapter 8: nineteen of the Queens' slices (Humpty Dumpty, the Lion, the Unicorn, Alicia, the Jabberwock, the Tweedles, the Bandersnatch and the others), fifteen shells of the White Queen and nine layers of the Red Queen; D86 is named Kagemusha throughout. 117 pages.

Version 2 added two chapters: Face to Face (#77), the new law of Aristotle's pyramids, after the five-pyramids chapter (now Chapter 4), and Between the Queens (#76), the five stages from the 600-cell to the 120-cell (Chapter 7); the book now shows eight results.

"Why, sometimes I've believed as many as six impossible things before breakfast." (the White Queen, Lewis Carroll, Through the Looking-Glass, 1871)

A book on two regular solids of four-dimensional space, seen by their shadows and slices: the 600-cell, which DICTO named the White Queen, and its polar partner the 120-cell, the Red Queen, with the work that led to them. Five papers and one chapter first published here, in three parts, with an opening, a conclusion, open problems, an index and an About the author page.

The opening joins Alicia Boole Stott (1860–1940), who learned to see the fourth dimension and published the slices of the 600-cell and the 120-cell in 1900, and Charles Dodgson (Lewis Carroll, 1832–1898), whose Red and White Queens give the book its names; and it tells where DICTO's own work began, picturing rays from the centre of twelve dodecahedra round a thirteenth passing out through gaps that close in the fourth dimension, which led to his radial cell projection, an independent rediscovery of the classical reflection construction.

It shows six things. (1) Three small pieces, AXE, CLEO and FUJI, close the gaps between thirteen icosahedra (#19). (2) Of Aristotle's five face pyramids, exactly the cube's alone, the tetrahedron's with the octahedron's, or these three together fill space (#44). (3) Face to face the five pyramids keep to their own solids, and glued together DICTO's pieces make no new deltahedron up to four pieces (Chapter 3, first published in this book). (4) The triangle-faced shadows and slices of the 5-, 16-, 24- and 600-cell give variants of the convex deltahedra that join differently and new deltahedra with equal edges (#62). (5) The White Queen complete: 62 slice patterns in four directions, twelve all triangles, shadows resolved into exact halves, and fifteen Cleo shells round one corner (#63). (6) Aristotle's five pyramids are exactly the cores of the four-dimensional regular solids, seen in perspective, in polar pairs; the Red Queen is built exactly from the White Queen (#65).

The cover is the WONDER square: WONDER across and down a 6 × 6 square, each letter on a shape of the book (the White and Red Queens' shadows, Alicia, Alice, Humpty Dumpty, the White Rabbit), each letter in its partner's colour.

The ideas and names are DICTO's. Computation and proof with Claude (Anthropic). Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com.
